# Start here

Open this file in RStudio. Run the setup first, then the sections in order.
To reproduce everything from scratch, restart R and **Run All** or **Render**.
All data below are simulated teaching examples; no downloads are required.
The household example illustrates a design feature of Gerber, Green, and
Larimer (2008), **not a replication of their results**.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))
blue <- "#006D9C"
orange <- "#BA4A27"
B <- 4000
```

# 1. A null model we can count

Eight cups: four milk-first, four tea-first. The taster selects exactly four
as milk-first. Let $K$ be the number of actual milk-first cups in that selection.
Under random guessing, every set of four is equally likely.

$$P_0(K=k)=\frac{\binom{4}{k}\binom{4}{4-k}}{\binom{8}{4}}.$$

```{r}
#| label: tea-exact
tea <- data.frame(k = 0:4)
tea$prob <- choose(4, tea$k) * choose(4, 4 - tea$k) / choose(8, 4)
tea
sum(tea$prob)
p_tea <- sum(tea$prob[tea$k >= 4])
p_tea
```

This is an **upper-tail** test: successful discrimination gives large $K$.
With perfect performance, $p=1/70$. If $K=3$, the tail includes both 3 and 4,
so $p=17/70$, not merely $P_0(K=3)$.

```{r}
#| label: tea-simulate
set.seed(21101)
cups <- c(rep("milk-first", 4), rep("tea-first", 4))
k_sim <- replicate(10000, {
  selected <- sample(cups, size = 4, replace = FALSE)
  sum(selected == "milk-first")
})
mean(k_sim >= 4)

p_tea_plot <- ggplot(tea, aes(k, prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue, width = .65) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4) +
  labs(x = "K: milk-first cups correctly selected", y = "Null probability")
p_tea_plot
```

# 2. One sample: statistic, p-value, and confidence interval

Suppose a political attitude score has population mean $\mu$. Test
$H_0:\mu=50$ against $H_A:\mu\ne50$. The simulation below deliberately uses
independent Normal observations, so the one-sample t reference is exact.
In other settings, the studentized CLT can justify approximate inference.

```{r}
#| label: one-sample
set.seed(21102)
score <- rnorm(50, mean = 54, sd = 12)
n <- length(score)
se <- sd(score) / sqrt(n)
t_obs <- (mean(score) - 50) / se
p_manual <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), df = n - 1)
ci_manual <- mean(score) + c(-1, 1) * qt(.975, df = n - 1) * se
one_fit <- t.test(score, mu = 50)

c(mean = mean(score), SE = se, t = t_obs, p = p_manual)
ci_manual
one_fit
```

The two-sided p-value counts both tails beyond $\pm|t_{obs}|$.
Does the 95% interval contain 50? Does the test reject at $\alpha=.05$?
These decisions agree when we use the same SE, reference distribution, and
confidence level. A one-sided alternative would need to be chosen **before**
seeing the direction of the result; `alternative = "greater"` tests $\mu>50$.

```{r}
#| label: p-value-plot
ref <- data.frame(t = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 2001))
ref$density <- dt(ref$t, df = n - 1)
p_pvalue <- ggplot(ref, aes(t, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(ref, t <= -abs(t_obs)), fill = orange, alpha = .6) +
  geom_area(data = subset(ref, t >= abs(t_obs)), fill = orange, alpha = .6) +
  geom_line(color = blue, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(t_obs), abs(t_obs)), linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Test statistic under H0", y = "Density",
       subtitle = sprintf("Shaded null probability = %.4f", p_manual))
p_pvalue
```

# 3. Two independent samples: Welch's test

Compare independent samples from two populations of attitude scores.
Define the contrast as **Y minus X**. Unequal sample sizes and variances are
allowed. These synthetic samples do not by themselves establish a causal effect.

```{r}
#| label: welch
set.seed(21103)
x <- rnorm(30, mean = 50, sd = 10)
y <- rnorm(45, mean = 56, sd = 16)
d_hat <- mean(y) - mean(x)
se_diff <- sqrt(var(y) / length(y) + var(x) / length(x))
welch_fit <- t.test(y, x, mu = 0)

c(difference = d_hat, SE = se_diff, statistic = d_hat / se_diff)
welch_fit
```

R's default is Welch's method (`var.equal = FALSE`). It uses a t reference
with approximate degrees of freedom. It does **not** require equal population
variances, but it still needs the observations and the groups to be independent
for this SE formula. It does not solve dependence or confounding.

# 4. Paired observations: analyze the differences

The same 20 respondents answer before and after a debate. A respondent's
baseline attitude appears in both measurements. Responses within a person
are related; the **people** are independent in this simulation.

```{r}
#| label: paired
set.seed(21104)
before <- rnorm(20, mean = 50, sd = 12)
after <- before + rnorm(20, mean = 3, sd = 5)
change <- after - before
paired_fit <- t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
change_fit <- t.test(change, mu = 0)
paired_fit
change_fit
c(paired_SE = sd(change) / sqrt(length(change)),
  ignoring_pairs_SE = sqrt(var(after) / length(after) +
                             var(before) / length(before)))
```

Here pairing reduces the SE because the before/after covariance is positive.
That is a property of these data, not a guarantee for every pair of variables.
A before/after comparison alone does not isolate the debate's causal effect.

```{r}
#| label: paired-plot
paired_data <- data.frame(id = rep(1:20, 2),
                          time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), each = 20),
                                        levels = c("Before", "After")),
                          score = c(before, after))
p_pairs <- ggplot(paired_data, aes(time, score, group = id)) +
  geom_line(color = blue, alpha = .5) + geom_point(color = blue) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attitude score", subtitle = "One line connects one respondent's two answers")
p_pairs
```

# 5. Power: repeat an entire study

Imagine two independent groups of attitude scores with a common population
SD of 10. Let $\delta=\mu_Y-\mu_X$ be the true difference and let `n_group`
be the sample size **in each group**. We simulate the same Welch test we would
use to analyze a study. Record whether each fresh study rejects $H_0:\delta=0$.

```{r}
#| label: power-function
reject_once <- function(n_group, delta, sigma = 10, alpha = .05) {
  x_new <- rnorm(n_group, mean = 50, sd = sigma)
  y_new <- rnorm(n_group, mean = 50 + delta, sd = sigma)
  t.test(y_new, x_new)$p.value < alpha
}

set.seed(21105)
power_grid <- expand.grid(n_group = c(30, 60, 120), delta = c(0, 3, 6))
power_grid$rejection_rate <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(power_grid)), function(i) {
  mean(replicate(B, reject_once(power_grid$n_group[i], power_grid$delta[i])))
}, numeric(1))
power_grid$MCSE <- sqrt(power_grid$rejection_rate *
                         (1 - power_grid$rejection_rate) / B)
power_grid
```

At $\delta=0$, the rejection rate estimates the Type I error rate. At a
specified nonzero $\delta$, it estimates power. More simulated repetitions
reduce **Monte Carlo error**; more subjects per group change the study's power.

## A Normal approximation for the graph

For these planning assumptions, the population SE of the difference is
$s=10\sqrt{2/n}$. Approximate its sampling distribution by $N(\delta,s^2)$
and reject when $|\widehat D|>1.96s$. The rejection cutoffs come from the null;
we evaluate their probability under each alternative.

```{r}
#| label: normal-power
normal_power <- function(delta, n_group, sigma = 10, alpha = .05) {
  s <- sigma * sqrt(2 / n_group)
  cutoff <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) * s
  pnorm(-cutoff, mean = delta, sd = s) +
    pnorm(cutoff, mean = delta, sd = s, lower.tail = FALSE)
}

power_curves <- expand.grid(delta = seq(0, 10, by = .1),
                           n_group = c(30, 60, 120))
power_curves$power <- with(power_curves, normal_power(delta, n_group))
p_power_curves <- ggplot(power_curves,
                        aes(delta, power, color = factor(n_group))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = power_grid, aes(y = rejection_rate), size = 2.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .05, linetype = 3, color = "gray50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(blue, orange, "#47733D"), name = "n per group") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "True mean difference (score points)", y = "Probability of rejection",
       subtitle = "Lines: Normal approximation; points: simulated Welch tests")
p_power_curves
```

The small gaps also reflect that Welch's test estimates the SE and uses a
t cutoff; the curves use the population SE and a Normal cutoff.

## Planning a sample size in R

`power.t.test()` provides a convenient calculation for a balanced, common-SD
Normal model using the pooled two-sample t test. This is a planning model;
it is not an exact power calculation for every design or for unequal-variance
Welch tests. Simulation lets us explore the procedure and design we actually intend.

```{r}
#| label: power-plan
plan <- power.t.test(delta = 3, sd = 10, power = .80,
                     sig.level = .05, type = "two.sample",
                     alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
plan
ceiling(plan$n)  # Round up: number needed IN EACH GROUP.
```

`strict = TRUE` counts rejections in either tail, as a two-sided test does.
Plan around a substantively meaningful effect and plausible variability,
not the observed effect from the study whose p-value you are interpreting.

# 6. Bootstrap: approximate sampling uncertainty

Reuse the 50 attitude scores from Section 2. Treat their empirical distribution
(each observed score gets probability $1/n$) as a stand-in for the unknown
population. Draw samples of size $n$ **with replacement**, recomputing the mean.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-mean
set.seed(21106)
boot_mean <- replicate(B, {
  score_star <- sample(score, size = length(score), replace = TRUE)
  mean(score_star)
})
c(estimate = mean(score), bootstrap_SE = sd(boot_mean),
  formula_SE = sd(score) / sqrt(length(score)))
quantile(boot_mean, c(.025, .975))  # Approximate percentile interval.

p_boot_mean <- ggplot(data.frame(estimate = boot_mean), aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(score), color = orange, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean in a bootstrap sample", y = "Number of replicates",
       subtitle = "The bootstrap distribution is centered near the observed sample mean")
p_boot_mean
```

The bootstrap SD estimates the estimator's standard error. The percentile
interval is an approximate method, not an exact coverage guarantee. These
replicates fluctuate around the observed mean, **not around the null mean 50**.
Counting how often `boot_mean` exceeds the observed mean would not give a
valid p-value for $H_0:\mu=50$.

This is the idea behind the bootstrap summaries provided in B4. It can also
help with statistics whose SE formulas are less familiar, such as a median
or ratio. Its validity still depends on the sampling structure and statistic.

# 7. Dependence: keep households together

Gerber, Green, and Larimer assigned treatment at the household level, within
geographic blocks. Our **synthetic illustration** uses a simpler design:
60 independent households, two voters each, and exactly 30 treated households.
Potential outcomes are fixed once generated; assignment determines which we see.

The latent household propensity creates related outcomes within a household.
The optional details of generating potential outcomes are shown here so the
example is completely reproducible; the resampling starts with `voters`.

```{r}
#| label: household-data
set.seed(21107)
H <- 60
household_propensity <- rbeta(H, shape1 = .3, shape2 = .7)
household <- rep(seq_len(H), each = 2)
u <- runif(2 * H)
p0 <- household_propensity[household]
p1 <- plogis(qlogis(p0) + .6)
y0 <- as.integer(u < p0)
y1 <- as.integer(u < p1)
assigned <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = H / 2))
voters <- data.frame(household, treated = assigned[household],
                     voted = ifelse(assigned[household] == 1, y1, y0))

hh <- voters |>
  group_by(household, treated) |>
  summarise(turnout = mean(voted), .groups = "drop")
head(voters)
head(hh)
```

Each household mean is 0, 0.5, or 1. Because every household has two voters,
the mean of household means equals the mean across voters in that arm.
With unequal household sizes, averaging household rates and averaging voters
can target different quantities; preserve the intended weighting.

```{r}
#| label: household-bootstrap
h_treated <- hh$turnout[hh$treated == 1]
h_control <- hh$turnout[hh$treated == 0]
observed <- mean(h_treated) - mean(h_control)

set.seed(21108)
boot_household <- replicate(B, {
  t_star <- sample(h_treated, length(h_treated), replace = TRUE)
  c_star <- sample(h_control, length(h_control), replace = TRUE)
  mean(t_star) - mean(c_star)
})
observed
sd(boot_household)
```

We resample household summaries **within each arm**, with replacement. For
this equal-size, mean-outcome example, that preserves exactly the contribution
of resampling whole households with all their voters. This bootstrap models
sampling independent households; it is not the experiment's reassignment test.

## Compare with resampling individual voters

```{r}
#| label: naive-bootstrap
v_treated <- voters$voted[voters$treated == 1]
v_control <- voters$voted[voters$treated == 0]
set.seed(21109)
boot_voter <- replicate(B, {
  mean(sample(v_treated, length(v_treated), replace = TRUE)) -
    mean(sample(v_control, length(v_control), replace = TRUE))
})
bootstrap_comparison <- data.frame(
  resampling_unit = c("Individual voter", "Whole household"),
  bootstrap_SE = c(sd(boot_voter), sd(boot_household)))
bootstrap_comparison

boot_comparison <- data.frame(
  estimate = c(boot_voter, boot_household),
  unit = rep(c("Individual voter", "Whole household"), each = B))
p_cluster_boot <- ggplot(boot_comparison, aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 60, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed, color = orange, linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~unit, nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-.2, 0, .2, .4)) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap difference in turnout proportions", y = "Number of replicates")
p_cluster_boot
```

The row bootstrap breaks the positive within-household association and
understates uncertainty here. This is the same dependence issue as repeated
responses in A6. More rows need not mean more independent information.

# 8. A null distribution from randomized assignments

For the synthetic experiment, consider the **sharp null**: treatment changes
no voter's outcome, $Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every voter. Under that null, the
observed outcomes would be the same under every allowed assignment. Keep them
fixed; randomly assign exactly 30 of the 60 **households** to treatment again.

```{r}
#| label: household-randomization
set.seed(21110)
null_difference <- replicate(B, {
  d_star <- sample(hh$treated, replace = FALSE)
  mean(hh$turnout[d_star == 1]) - mean(hh$turnout[d_star == 0])
})
# Count ties as at least as extreme; tolerance handles floating-point rounding.
extreme <- abs(null_difference) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12
p_randomization <- (1 + sum(extreme)) / (B + 1)
c(observed_difference = observed, randomization_p = p_randomization)

p_randomization_plot <- ggplot(data.frame(difference = null_difference),
                              aes(difference)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 60, fill = blue, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(observed), abs(observed)),
             color = orange, linewidth = 1, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Difference under reassigned household labels", y = "Number of replicates",
       subtitle = sprintf("Two-sided Monte Carlo p-value = %.3f", p_randomization))
p_randomization_plot
```

Unlike the bootstrap, these labels are shuffled **without replacement**:
every household appears once and the treatment count is unchanged. The `+1`
correction includes the observed assignment in the Monte Carlo calculation
and avoids a reported p-value of zero. Full enumeration would use its exact
tail proportion instead.

A sharp null is stronger than a zero **average** effect: positive and negative
individual effects could cancel. This simple randomization test is justified
by the sharp null and the assignment design (also assuming no interference
between households). It is not a generic exact test of equal means for
arbitrary observational groups.

**For the actual Gerber–Green–Larimer design**, reassign households within the
original blocks and retain each block's treatment-arm counts. Do not apply
our unrestricted two-arm shuffle to their data.

# 9. Choose the repetition to match the question

| Goal | What gets repeated? | What remains fixed? |
|---|---|---|
| Power | Generate fresh studies under a specified true effect | Design, analysis rule, and model parameters |
| Bootstrap SE | Sample units with replacement from observed data | Sample size and the chosen resampling structure |
| Randomization test | Draw assignments allowed by the design | Outcomes under the sharp null, units, and design constraints |

For paired data, resample pairs. For households or schools, preserve clusters.
For serial dependence, a suitable block or time-series method is needed.
Resampling is not a repair for a biased sample, confounding, or too few independent units.
